content: Actin is a globular protein with a molecular weight of approximately 42 kDa, found in all eukaryotic cells except nematode sperm. It is present at high concentrations, often exceeding 100 μM. Actin is one of the most highly conserved proteins across species, with less than 20% sequence variation between organisms as diverse as algae and humans. It serves as the monomeric subunit of microfilaments, which are one of the three primary components of the cytoskeleton. In muscle cells, actin is a key component of thin filaments, which are integral to the contractile apparatus. Actin plays a critical role in numerous cellular processes, including muscle contraction, cell motility, cell division, cytokinesis, vesicle and organelle transport, cell signaling, and the establishment and maintenance of cell junctions and shape. Actin filaments are linked to α-actinin and the cell membrane via vinculin. The head domain of vinculin interacts with E-cadherin through α-, β-, and γ-catenins, while its tail domain binds to membrane lipids and actin filaments. At the genetic level, actin exhibits 2% sequence conservation between humans and the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, while the primary structure of the protein product is 95% conserved. Most yeast species have a single actin gene, whereas higher eukaryotes express multiple actin isoforms encoded by a family of related genes. Mammals, for instance, have at least six actin isoforms, categorized into three classes—alpha, beta, and gamma—based on their isoelectric points. Alpha actins are predominantly found in muscle tissues (e.g., skeletal, aortic smooth, cardiac, and enteric smooth muscle), while beta and gamma isoforms are more common in non-muscle cells. Despite their similar amino acid sequences and in vitro properties, these isoforms are not fully interchangeable in vivo. The typical actin gene consists of a 5' untranslated region (UTR) of approximately 100 nucleotides, a translated region of about 1200 nucleotides, and a 3' UTR of around 200 nucleotides. Most actin genes are interrupted by introns, with up to six introns located in any of 19 well-characterized positions. The high conservation of the actin family makes it a preferred model for studying intron evolution, particularly in comparing the introns-early and introns-late models. Non-spherical prokaryotes possess actin-like genes, such as MreB, which are essential for maintaining cell shape. Additionally, the plasmid-derived gene ParM encodes an actin-like protein that dynamically partitions plasmid DNA into daughter cells during cell division, functioning analogously to microtubules in eukaryotic mitosis. Actin is present in both smooth and rough endoplasmic reticulum. It has three primary functions in cells: (1) to form the most dynamic component of the cytoskeleton, providing mechanical support and facilitating signal transduction by connecting the cytoplasm to the surrounding environment; (2) to enable cell motility, as seen in processes like actoclampin molecular motors; and (3) to generate force in conjunction with myosin proteins, supporting muscle contraction, vesicle transport, and other intracellular transport processes. Individual actin subunits, known as globular actin (G-actin), polymerize into long filamentous polymers called filamentous actin (F-actin). Two parallel F-actin strands twist into a helical structure, forming microfilaments that are approximately 7 nm in diameter, with a helical repeat every 37 nm. The polarity of an actin filament can be determined by decorating it with myosin S1 fragments, which create barbed (+) and pointed (-) ends. An S1 fragment consists of the head and neck domains of myosin II. In muscle cells, actin is the primary component of thin filaments, which, together with myosin (the motor protein forming thick filaments), are organized into actomyosin myofibrils. These myofibrils drive muscle contraction. Myosin heads hydrolyze ATP to generate energy, undergoing a cycle of attachment to thin filaments, tension exertion, and power strokes that slide the thin filaments past one another, shortening the muscle. In contractile bundles, the actin-bundling protein alpha-actinin spaces thin filaments approximately 35 nm apart, allowing thick filaments to fit between them and interact, enabling deformation or contraction. During deformation, one end of myosin is anchored to the plasma membrane, while the other end walks toward the plus end of the actin filament, reshaping the membrane relative to the cell cortex. In contraction, myosin molecules bind to two separate filaments and simultaneously walk toward their respective plus ends, sliding the actin filaments closer together and shortening the actin bundle. This mechanism underlies muscle contraction and cytokinesis, the division of one cell into two. Actin polymerization and depolymerization are essential for chemotaxis and cytokinesis, with nucleating factors required to stimulate actin polymerization. Actin filaments themselves bind ATP, and ATP hydrolysis destabilizes the polymer. The discovery of actin is credited to Brúnó F. Straub, a biochemist in Albert Szent-Györgyi's laboratory at the University of Szeged, Hungary. In 1942, Straub developed a method for extracting muscle protein, isolating substantial amounts of relatively pure actin. This method remains in use today. Szent-Györgyi had previously described a more viscous form of myosin as activated myosin, and since Straub's protein produced this activating effect, it was named actin. Due to World War II, their findings were not published in Western scientific journals until 1945, when they appeared as a supplement to Acta Physiologica Scandinavica. Straub continued his work on actin and, in 1950, reported that actin contains bound ATP, which is hydrolyzed to ADP and inorganic phosphate during polymerization into microfilaments. He suggested that the transformation of ATP-bound actin to ADP-bound actin played a role in muscle contraction, a hypothesis later confirmed for smooth muscle in 2001. The crystal structure of G-actin was solved in 1990 by Kabsch and colleagues, and a model for F-actin was proposed the same year by Holmes and colleagues, based on low-resolution fiber diffraction data. While several filament models have since been proposed, a high-resolution X-ray structure of F-actin remains unavailable. Certain bacteria, such as Listeria, exploit the host cell's actin machinery for intracellular movement. The bacterial ActA transmembrane protein induces directed actin polymerization, propelling the bacterial cell within the host.
